title: That Is Not Who I Am
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece challenges the habit of treating changeable behaviors as fixed personality traits. It distinguishes a genuinely short list of stable, biologically rooted traits from the much larger set of learned behaviors, like conflict avoidance or indecisiveness, that people wrongly declare immutable. The article draws a key linguistic distinction between "this is not who I am" (a surrender to a fixed identity) and "this is not who I like to be" (an acknowledgment that growth requires discomfort). It closes with a direct challenge to stop using fixed-mindset language as an excuse to avoid personal development.
points: Separates truly fixed, biologically rooted traits from learned behaviors misclassified as fixed
Gives examples of self-limiting phrases people use to avoid personal change
Draws a key distinction between "who I am" and "who I like to be"
Challenges readers to reject fixed-mindset excuses and commit to development
quotes: The traits and predispositions that make us who we are are tied deeply to our biology and heredity.
Whenever we tell ourselves, “My personality is one that avoids conflict,” or “Decisive is not who I am,” we give ourselves the ultimate excuse not to improve.
There is a tremendous difference between the expressions “This is not who I am,” and “This is not who I like to be.
The former is a flag of surrender. The latter is an acknowledgment that we need to push ourselves to grow by engaging in more situations that create discomfort.
Self-improvement begins with a rejection of the fixed mindset of who we are.
So stop letting yourself off the hook for making personal change. Your development depends on it.
